title: NURS 1021 Unit 1 Case Study 4

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which of the following findings would be consistent with iron deficiency anemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Urge to move the legs when lying in bed at night
Seasonal allergies treated with loratadine
No numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
Pale conjunctivae with a heart rate of 108 beats/min
Craving and chewing ice
Thin, spoon-shaped fingernails
Tiredness and shortness of breath on one flight of stairs
Cracks at the corners of the mouth and a smooth, sore tongue

question.explanation:
Consistent with iron deficiency anemia: with less hemoglobin, the blood carries less oxygen, causing tiredness and dyspnea on exertion (Option 7), pallor, and a faster heart rate (with a flow murmur) as the heart compensates (Option 4). Severe iron deficiency also causes pica, a craving for non-food items, most often ice (pagophagia) (Option 5); koilonychia, thin spoon-shaped nails (Option 6); angular cheilitis and glossitis (Option 8); and restless legs syndrome, an unpleasant urge to move the legs at rest (Option 1).

Not consistent: the absence of numbness and tingling is a relevant negative: neurologic symptoms with anemia suggest vitamin B12 deficiency, not iron deficiency (Option 3). Seasonal allergies are unrelated (Option 2).

leftContent.intro: The nurse in a primary care clinic is assessing Amara, a 34-year-old female client who reports increasing tiredness over the past 4 months.

question.stem: The nurse explains how microcytic anemias are told apart. For each finding, click to specify whether it is most consistent with iron deficiency anemia, beta-thalassemia trait, or anemia of chronic disease.

rows.text: Raised hemoglobin A2 on hemoglobin electrophoresis
Low serum iron with normal or low TIBC and normal or high ferritin, in a client with rheumatoid arthritis
Total iron-binding capacity above the reference range
Marked microcytosis with a normal RDW and a normal or high red cell count
Mild anemia with normal-sized red cells that develops over months of chronic inflammation

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 1100 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Iron deficiency anemia: iron stores are used up first, so ferritin (stored iron) falls; a ferritin below 30 µg/L is specific for iron deficiency. The liver makes more transferrin to capture what iron there is, so the TIBC rises while serum iron and transferrin saturation fall. Only then are red cells made small and pale, with a wide range of sizes (high RDW). Amara has all of these: ferritin 4 µg/L, TIBC 88 µmol/L, saturation 0.05, MCV 68 fL, RDW 19.8%. The low reticulocyte count shows the marrow cannot respond without iron, and a raised platelet count is common in iron deficiency.

Beta-thalassemia trait: reduced beta-globin chain production makes small cells even though iron is normal, so ferritin is normal. Cells are uniformly small (normal RDW) and the marrow makes more of them, so the red cell count is normal or high. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows a raised HbA2. Her low ferritin and high RDW point to iron deficiency; thalassemia trait can coexist and is checked once iron is replaced if microcytosis persists.

Anemia of chronic disease: inflammation raises hepcidin, which traps iron in stores. Serum iron is low but ferritin is normal or high and the TIBC normal or low. The anemia is usually mild and normocytic.

leftContent.intro: Amara returns the next day to review her blood work.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: Amara's anemia is caused by [[drop0]], so her marrow makes small, pale red cells with too little hemoglobin. The main reason her iron stores are depleted is [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority concern is [[drop2]].

options.text: too little vitamin B12 to make DNA
failure of the bone marrow stem cells
too little iron to make hemoglobin
early destruction of red cells
loratadine blocking iron absorption
a vegan diet that contains no iron
ongoing blood loss from heavy menstrual bleeding
an inherited defect in globin chains
a risk of falls from dizziness and reduced oxygen delivery
an altered body image from nail changes
nerve damage from vitamin deficiency
a risk of bleeding from a low platelet count

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 1130 and the Vital Signs.
question.explanation:
Pathogenesis: iron is needed to build heme. Without it, red cell precursors keep dividing while they wait for hemoglobin, so the cells end up small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic). Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and makes large cells; hemolysis and marrow failure have other laboratory patterns.

Cause: in a premenopausal woman, menstrual loss is the most common cause; each 1 mL of blood holds about 0.5 mg of iron, and heavy bleeding (here from fibroids) loses several times the normal amount every cycle. Her vegan diet adds to the problem because plant (non-heme) iron is absorbed less well than iron from meat, but plant foods do contain iron. Iron therapy without finding the source of loss is poor practice, so the fibroids are referred to gynecology. Loratadine does not affect iron absorption; her ferritin rules out thalassemia as the cause.

Priority: her heart rate rises 16 beats/min on standing, she has had dizziness, and she climbs ladders at work: reduced oxygen-carrying capacity puts her at risk of falls and injury. Her platelet count is high, not low, and she has no neurologic signs.

question.stem: Which instructions should the nurse include in Amara's teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take two tablets the next day if you miss a dose
Take the iron tablet 30 minutes before a meal, with a glass of orange juice
Take the tablet with a glass of milk to prevent an upset stomach
Take the tablet at least 2 hours apart from milk, tea, coffee and antacids
Drink more fluids and eat more fibre if you become constipated
Eat beans, lentils, tofu and iron-fortified cereals with foods rich in vitamin C
Stop taking the iron once you no longer feel tired
Expect your stools to turn dark green or black while taking iron

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 1145.
question.explanation:
Include: iron is absorbed best on an empty stomach, about 30 minutes before meals; vitamin C (orange juice or a 500 mg tablet) keeps iron in the absorbable ferrous form (Option 2). Calcium in milk, tannins in tea, polyphenols in coffee, antacids and some antibiotics bind iron, so they are separated from the dose (Option 4). Dark green or black stools are an expected, harmless effect; tarry stools with abdominal pain or dizziness are reported (Option 8). A vegan diet can supply enough iron if non-heme sources are eaten with vitamin C (Option 6). Constipation is the most common adverse effect (Option 5).

Do not include: milk reduces absorption (Option 3). Feeling better comes before the stores are refilled; iron continues for about 6 months after the hemoglobin is normal (Option 7). Doubling a dose increases nausea and constipation and is not absorbed well; every-other-day dosing is used because each dose raises hepcidin, which blocks the absorption of the next one for about a day (Option 1).

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated for the IV iron infusion.

rows.text: Take vital signs before the infusion and monitor during it
Check the IV site for patency and leakage during the infusion
Give the iron by intramuscular injection if the IV insertion is difficult
Give a test dose of iron sucrose before the first full dose
Observe Amara for at least 30 minutes after the infusion
Tell Amara to take her iron tablets on infusion days for a faster response

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Week 4 1000 and the Vital Signs.
question.explanation:
Indicated: IV iron can cause hypersensitivity reactions (flushing, chest tightness, dyspnea, hypotension), so vital signs are taken before and during the infusion and the client is observed for at least 30 minutes after; the infusion is stopped and help called at the first sign of a reaction. Leakage of iron into the tissues causes pain and long-lasting brown staining of the skin, so the site is checked throughout.

Non-Essential: current iron sucrose products do not need a test dose; test doses were used with the old high-molecular-weight iron dextran.

Contraindicated: iron sucrose is given only IV; intramuscular iron is painful, stains the skin and is no longer used. Oral iron is not combined with IV iron; IV iron raises hepcidin, so oral iron would be poorly absorbed and would only add adverse effects.

leftContent.intro: Four weeks later, Amara returns for follow-up.

question.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate that the treatment of Amara's anemia has been effective.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Week 12 1000, the Vital Signs, and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Effective: more energy and climbing stairs without stopping show better oxygen delivery, as do a heart rate down from 108 to 82 beats/min. Hemoglobin rose from 86 to 121 g/L and ferritin from 4 to 142 µg/L, showing that the stores are refilled (with IV iron, ferritin rises quickly). Pica, restless legs and angular cheilitis resolve as iron is replaced.

Not yet evidence of effect: nails take months to grow out, so spoon-shaped nails persist for some time. The MCV (79 fL) is still slightly low because cells made before treatment are still circulating; it normalizes as they are replaced over about 120 days. Ongoing heavy bleeding is the cause, which iron does not treat: without gynecologic treatment of the fibroids, she will become iron deficient again.
